questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a rising old-age dependency ratio
questions.stem: In a workplace report, a region's old-age dependency ratio rose from 18 to 24 over a decade. What does this change most directly indicate?

options.text: Each one hundred working-age people now support more people aged sixty-five and over.
The region now has fewer children than it did ten years ago.
options.misconception: mixes the old-age ratio with the youth dependency ratio

options.text: The working-age group now supports more older adults for every one hundred workers.
options.misconception: confuses the ratio with the total count of elderly residents

options.text: The region's total population fell by roughly one quarter.
options.misconception: reads a percentage-point shift as a population decline

questions.explanation: The old-age dependency ratio compares people aged sixty-five and over with the working-age population. A rise from 18 to 24 means more dependents per one hundred workers, not fewer children or a falling total.
questions.hint: Compare dependents aged 65+ with workers aged 15-64.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Net migration from a flows table
questions.learningObjective: Compute net migration from in and out flows
questions.stem: A workplace report table shows 4,200 people moved into a city and 3,500 moved out during one year. What is the net migration?
questions.explanation: Net migration equals in-migration minus out-migration. 4,200 minus 3,500 gives 700, a net inflow. Reversing the subtraction would give a negative and wrong sign.
questions.hint: Subtract outflows from inflows.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.learningObjective: Define remittances in a migration context
questions.stem: A workplace report on labor migration mentions remittances sent home by workers abroad. What are remittances?

options.text: Taxes paid by migrants to their host country's government.
options.misconception: confuses remittances with fiscal obligations abroad

options.text: Money or goods migrants send back to family or communities at home.
Loans taken by migrants from banks in the destination country.
options.misconception: treats remittances as borrowed credit rather than transfers

options.text: Profits earned by firms hiring migrant labor.
options.misconception: confuses household transfers with corporate earnings

questions.explanation: Remittances are funds or goods that migrants transmit to their origin households or communities. They are not taxes, loans, or corporate profits, though each is a money flow nearby in the same report.
questions.hint: Think of money flowing back to origin households.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why equal populations can differ in age structure
questions.stem: Two cities have the same total population, yet one has far more school-age children. Explain in a workplace report why totals alone mislead.

answer.exemplar: Equal totals can hide very different age distributions, so planning schools or clinics needs age breakdowns, not just population counts.

questions.explanation: A single total hides how people are distributed across ages. Services such as schools and clinics depend on age groups, so identical totals can imply very different needs.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.learningObjective: Define urbanization

stimulus.body: A workplace report notes that a country's share of residents living in urban areas rose from 35 percent to 52 percent between 1990 and 2020.

questions.stem: The report describes rising urbanization. Which statement best defines urbanization?

options.text: The total number of people living in all cities worldwide.
options.misconception: confuses urbanization with global urban population size

options.text: The movement of people from cities to rural areas.
options.misconception: reverses the direction of urbanization

options.text: The speed at which any single city grows each year.
options.misconception: confuses urbanization with city growth rate

options.text: The share of a population living in urban areas.

questions.explanation: Urbanization is the proportion of a population residing in urban areas. It is not a worldwide total, a single city's growth speed, or ruralward movement.
questions.hint: It is a share, not a count or speed.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish city growth rate from urbanization level
questions.stem: A report shows a city growing at 4% a year while national urbanization barely changed. What best explains the difference?

options.text: City growth measures one place; urbanization measures the national urban share.
Urbanization always rises when any city grows quickly.
options.misconception: assumes city growth automatically raises national urban share

options.text: A 4% city growth rate means the country is fully urbanized.
options.misconception: confuses a local rate with a national level

options.text: National urbanization ignores all cities under one million people.
options.misconception: invents a population threshold not in the report

questions.explanation: A single city can grow fast while the national urban share stays flat if rural areas also grow or if growth is offset by reclassification. The two measures answer different questions.
questions.hint: One is local, the other is national.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.learningObjective: Compute average annual growth rate
questions.stem: A city's population grew from 100,000 to 121,000 over two years. What is the average annual growth rate in percent?
questions.explanation: Growth factor over two years is 121,000 divided by 100,000, or 1.21. The square root is 1.10, so the average annual growth rate is 10 percent. Using simple division gives 10.5, which is slightly off.
questions.hint: Take the square root of the two-year growth factor.

options.misconception: names rural push or retention factors as pulls

options.text: Higher wages and more formal jobs available in urban centers.
Smaller family sizes required by city governments.
options.misconception: invents a policy requirement not mentioned

questions.explanation: Pull factors draw migrants toward destinations; higher wages and formal jobs are classic urban pulls. Fertile soil and land prices are rural attractions, while climate and invented policies are not the reported driver.

questions.learningObjective: Compute net migration rate
questions.stem: A city gained 2,000 migrants and lost 1,200 in one year, with a midyear population of 80,000. What is the net migration rate per 1,000 residents?

answer.exemplar: If rural population grows at a similar pace or boundaries change, the national urban share can stay flat even while individual cities expand rapidly.

options.text: 10 percent, from the square root of the two-year growth factor.
5 percent, from halving the total percentage increase.

options.text: County Q, because it has more older adults per worker.
Neither, because dependency ratios use only children.
options.misconception: misstates the dependency ratio formula

questions.explanation: With equal totals, the county with more residents aged 65+ has more dependents per worker, hence a higher old-age dependency ratio. Totals alone do not determine the ratio.
questions.hint: More older adults means higher dependency.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a rising urban share
questions.stem: A report notes urbanization rose from 45% to 60%. What does this indicate?

options.text: Rural population disappeared entirely.

options.text: A larger share of the population now lives in urban areas.

questions.explanation: A rising urbanization level means a larger share of the total population lives in urban areas. It does not require falling totals, empty rural areas, or a single city.

questions.stem: Urban population grew from 4 million to 4.4 million in one year. What is the annual growth rate in percent?

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.learningObjective: Explain a consequence of rural depopulation
questions.stem: A report links rural out-migration to abandoned farmland. Why might this happen?

answer.exemplar: When working-age adults leave, fewer people remain to farm the land, so some plots go uncultivated and rural economies shrink.

questions.explanation: Rural out-migration removes the labor needed for farming. With fewer workers, land may be abandoned and local economic activity declines, even if the land itself remains fertile.
questions.hint: Labor leaves, land stays.

questions.learningObjective: Explain a risk of remittance dependence

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.learningObjective: Explain when to use compound growth
questions.stem: A report compares two cities over several years. Why use compound annual growth rather than simple division?

answer.exemplar: Compound annual growth accounts for growth building on prior growth each year, while simple division ignores compounding and can misstate the yearly rate.

questions.explanation: Populations grow on previous levels, so the correct annual rate must compound. Simple division of total change by starting population treats growth as linear and can misstate the yearly rate.
questions.hint: Growth builds on prior growth.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why age structure matters more than totals
questions.stem: A report compares two equal-size populations with different age profiles. Why is age structure more informative than total size?
